sample.universe: All singletons born in Denmark from 1988 to 2002 (native Danes) with at least one sibling
sample.unit_of_observation: focal child (one observation per child; standard errors clustered at the matched group level)
selection_rules: identify all singletons born in Denmark 1988-2002 and their immediate family members from the population register
limit the sample to children born in 2002 or earlier so that they had time to finish compulsory schooling
restrict the sample to native Danes
delete all focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves
drop individuals from families where the focal child has more than one sibling diagnosed with T1D (0.61 percent of the sample)
treated focal children: those with one sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16
match (without replacement) each treated focal child to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size (3,068 of 3,070 treated children could be matched)
assign each non-treated focal child a pseudo year of onset equal to the onset date of the matched treated child's sibling
restrict the sample to sibling pairs where the focal child is at most five years older or younger than the sibling with T1D
do NOT condition on having taken the Danish language or mathematics 9th grade exit exam (so exam-outcome samples are smaller)
sample.n_observations: 13,752 focal children in the main matched sample (Exit Exam outcome samples range from 12,221 to 12,650; falsification sample 1,593; well-being sample 1,666-1,736)
sample.n_individuals: 13,752 focal children, of which 16.67 percent (2,292) have a sibling diagnosed with T1D and 11,460 do not

construction_notes: GPA is the average grade in the mandatory Danish language exams (oral and written) and the mandatory mathematics exam (written), standardized within each year

the GPA measure focuses on Danish and Mathematics because since 2007 the ministry has evaluated different versions of the other mandatory exams, and since 2015 a grade of at least 2 in mathematics and Danish is an entry requirement for vocational educations
'passed' is an indicator for a GPA in Danish and mathematics greater than or equal to 2, the cutoff for passing
'on-time graduation' is an indicator for completing 9th grade by age 16

'further education' is an indicator for being enrolled in high school or vocational school at any time before age 18; 'high school' is an indicator for the first post-elementary enrollment before age 18 being high school rather than vocational school, defined only for enrollees

mother and father characteristics are measured the year before the child is born, except 'child lives with one parent' (the year the child turns five) and parental age at birth (at childbirth); the note to Table 2 instead says parental characteristics are measured two years before the sibling's (pseudo) onset, and section 4.3 says the heterogeneity moderators are measured the year before the sibling's (pseudo) onset

employment is defined as wage income > 0; education is grouped into no qualifying education, short qualifying education (vocational training and academies of professional higher education) and long qualifying education (bachelor's degree and any graduate degree)

well-being outcomes are factor scores from an exploratory factor analysis (maximum likelihood, oblique promax rotation) of 33 items of the 2015-2017 National Well-being Survey (N = 708,323 for the factor analysis); items are standardized within grade and cohort and the final summated scores are standardized to mean zero and variance one
standard errors are clustered at the matched group level following Abadie and Spiess (2022)

claims.statement: A balance regression of the sibling-diabetes dummy on the full conditioning set yields a joint F-test of 0.963 (Prob > F = 0.517), i.e. no detectable difference between treated and control focal children on observables.

definition.value: Joint F-test of all regressors in the balance regression of the treatment dummy on the conditioning set.

timing.value: Matching variables and birth characteristics at birth; parental characteristics two years before the sibling's (pseudo) onset.

register_source.value: DanDiabKids (the clinical register of childhood and adolescent diabetes)

definition.value: Left-hand-side variable of the balance regression: the dummy for whether the focal child's sibling was diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turned 16.

timing.value: Diagnosis before the focal child turns 16; parental characteristics in the conditioning set are measured two years before the sibling's (pseudo) onset.

units.value: F-statistic of the joint test that all regressors are zero (dependent variable: sibling with diabetes 0/1)

estimand.target_population: Treated versus control focal children in the matched analysis sample

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). Table 2 regresses the treatment dummy on the full conditioning set as a balance test.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control).
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)

sibling spacing of three or fewer vs. four to five years
one vs. more than one sibling
mother has at least a bachelor's degree
mother's wage income in the bottom vs. top quartile

population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

the estimates are read as driven by time constraints rather than financial constraints in a Becker-Tomes type model

prior_findings_compared.citation: Black, Breining, Figlio, Guryan, Karbownik, Nielsen, & Simonsen (2021), 'Sibling spillovers', The Economic Journal
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: we find the total exposure to a disabled sibling leads to a decline of 3.8% of a standard deviation (with all covariates). The estimate is significant at a ten percent level.
Both Black et al. (2021) and this paper find very different results from Persson, Qui, and Rossin-Slater (2021), which focuses on marginal cases of ADHD and finds no impact on educational attainment.

prior_findings_compared.citation: Kristoffersen, Kraegpoeth, Nielsen, & Simonsen (2015) and Zhao & Zhao (2021) on disruptive peers
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: This suggests that having a sibling with T1D exerts a larger spillover to school performance than a disruptive peer, although the underlying mechanisms may be quite different (for instance teacher vs. parental investment).

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). The coefficient is the difference in the effect between male focal children and female focal children.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). The coefficient is the difference in the effect between male focal children and female focal children.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

This coefficient is the effect for focal children who are the younger sibling.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
subgroups_defined: Focal Child is an older sibling (0/1)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
falsification test using focal children whose sibling is diagnosed after the 9th grade Exit Exam (Table 4)
inclusion of matched group fixed effects (results not shown; available from the authors upon request)

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

definition.value: Indicator variable equal to one if the child is, at any time, enrolled into high school or vocational school before the age of 18.

estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children who are the younger sibling

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children who are the younger sibling.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
subgroups_defined: Focal Child is an older sibling (0/1)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children spaced three or fewer years from the sibling.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

register_source.value: DanDiabKids (the clinical register of childhood and adolescent diabetes; see Svensson et al., 2016)

definition.value: Dummy variable set equal to one if the focal child's sibling was diagnosed with T1D before the focal child was 16 years old. Diagnoses come from the clinical register DanDiabKids; each non-treated focal child is assigned a pseudo year of onset equal to the onset date of the matched treated child's sibling.

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

register_source.value: UDDA (Statistics Denmark): the education registry

definition.value: Indicator variable equal to one if the child is, at any time, enrolled into high school or vocational school before the age of 18.

timing.value: Enrollment at any time before age 18, after the sibling's T1D onset.

units.value: share of focal children (0/1 indicator outcome); 0.01 = 1 percentage point

estimand.target_population: focal children spaced three or fewer years from the sibling
estimand.time_horizon: enrollment measured at any time before age 18; the sibling's diagnosis occurs at any time before the focal child turns 16
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children spaced three or fewer years from the sibling

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children spaced three or fewer years from the sibling.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children with more than one sibling.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
falsification test using focal children whose sibling is diagnosed after the 9th grade Exit Exam (Table 4)

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). The coefficient is the difference in the effect between focal children whose mother has at least a bachelor's degree and focal children whose mother has less than a bachelor's degree.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
subgroups_defined: Mother has a bachelors degree or above (0/1)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)

unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.

The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

treatment.label: Diabetes (focal child's sibling diagnosed with type 1 diabetes)

register_source.value: DanDiabKids (the clinical register of childhood and adolescent diabetes; see Svensson et al., 2016)

definition.value: Dummy variable set equal to one if the focal child's sibling was diagnosed with T1D before the focal child was 16 years old. Diagnoses come from the clinical register DanDiabKids; each non-treated focal child is assigned a pseudo year of onset equal to the onset date of the matched treated child's sibling.

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

outcome.label: High School (high school vs. vocational school enrollment)

register_source.value: UDDA (Statistics Denmark): the education registry

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the first education enrolled into post elementary school and before the age of 18 was high school and equal to zero if the child instead enrolled into vocational school; defined only for those who enroll.

timing.value: First post-elementary enrollment before age 18, after the sibling's T1D onset.

units.value: share of focal children (0/1 indicator outcome); 0.01 = 1 percentage point

magnitude.interpretation: a 4.7 pp decrease in enrollment due to being a child of a lower educated mother and having a sibling with T1D

estimand.target_population: focal children whose mother has less than a bachelor's degree
estimand.time_horizon: enrollment measured at any time before age 18; the sibling's diagnosis occurs at any time before the focal child turns 16
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children whose mother has less than a bachelor's degree

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children whose mother has less than a bachelor's degree.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
subgroups_defined: Mother has a bachelors degree or above (0/1)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
