population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children whose mother is not employed.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children whose mother is employed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children whose mother is employed.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

The equation description on p. 6 says the adjusted regressions include maternal AND paternal age at birth, wage income and education, while the table notes say the regressions condition on 'characteristics pertaining the child and mother'; the control list recorded here follows p. 6.
Tables 5 and 6 report the moderator main effect only implicitly: the printed rows are '(1) diabetes', '(2) diabetes x moderator' and their sum '(1) + (2)'.
The legend under Table 6 prints '*** p<0.01, ** p<0.5, * p<0.1'; the ** threshold is read as p<0.05 by analogy with the paper's other tables.
The moderator is measured the year before the sibling's (pseudo) diabetes onset, while the covariates are measured the year before the child's birth.

definition.value: Dummy variable set equal to one if the focal child's sibling was diagnosed with T1D before the focal child was 16 years old. Diagnoses come from the clinical register DanDiabKids; each non-treated focal child is assigned a pseudo year of onset equal to the onset date of the matched treated child's sibling.

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

definition.value: Indicator variable equal to one if the child is, at any time, enrolled into high school or vocational school before the age of 18.

estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children whose mother is employed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children whose mother is employed.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed
robustness_checks: estimates reported with and without covariate adjustment (Table 3)
balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
falsification test using focal children whose sibling is diagnosed after the 9th grade Exit Exam (Table 4)
inclusion of matched group fixed effects (results not shown; available from the authors upon request)
Oster (2019) omitted-variable-bias methodology (results not shown; available upon request)

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). The coefficient is the difference in the effect between focal children whose mother is in the top quartile of the wage distribution and focal children whose mother is in the bottom quartile of the wage distribution.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children in two-parent households.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

estimand.target_population: focal children in two-parent households
estimand.time_horizon: 9th grade Exit Exam outcomes measured the year the child turns 16; the sibling's diagnosis occurs at any time before the focal child turns 16
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children in two-parent households

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). This coefficient is the effect for focal children in two-parent households.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.ages: outcomes measured at age 16 (9th grade Exit Exam) and by age 18 (enrollment)
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed

balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). Split by the focal child's age at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset; this column keeps focal children aged 13-15 yrs at onset, an age at which Danish children are lower secondary school (grades seven through nine).
population.ages: focal child aged 13-15 yrs at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset
subgroups_defined: focal child's age at the sibling's onset: 13-15 yrs
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). Split by the focal child's age at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset; this column keeps focal children aged 2-5 yrs at onset, an age at which Danish children are mostly placed in kindergarten.
population.ages: focal child aged 2-5 yrs at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset
subgroups_defined: focal child's age at the sibling's onset: 2-5 yrs
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed
robustness_checks: estimates reported with and without covariate adjustment (Table 3)
balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
falsification test using focal children whose sibling is diagnosed after the 9th grade Exit Exam (Table 4)
inclusion of matched group fixed effects (results not shown; available from the authors upon request)
Oster (2019) omitted-variable-bias methodology (results not shown; available upon request)

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

claims.statement: Among focal children aged 6-9 yrs at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset, having a sibling diagnosed with type 1 diabetes has no statistically significant effect on Any further education (enrollment) (coefficient 0.011).

treatment.label: Diabetes (focal child's sibling diagnosed with type 1 diabetes)

register_source.value: DanDiabKids (the clinical register of childhood and adolescent diabetes; see Svensson et al., 2016)

definition.value: Dummy variable set equal to one if the focal child's sibling was diagnosed with T1D before the focal child was 16 years old. Diagnoses come from the clinical register DanDiabKids; each non-treated focal child is assigned a pseudo year of onset equal to the onset date of the matched treated child's sibling.

timing.value: The sibling's T1D diagnosis occurs before the focal child turns 16, i.e. before the focal child sits the 9th grade Exit Exam.

register_source.value: UDDA (Statistics Denmark): the education registry

definition.value: Indicator variable equal to one if the child is, at any time, enrolled into high school or vocational school before the age of 18.

timing.value: Enrollment at any time before age 18, after the sibling's T1D onset.

units.value: share of focal children (0/1 indicator outcome); 0.01 = 1 percentage point

estimand.target_population: Focal children aged 6-9 yrs at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset
estimand.time_horizon: enrollment measured at any time before age 18; the sibling's diagnosis occurs at any time before the focal child turns 16; focal child aged 6-9 yrs at the sibling's onset
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Diabetes=1), G] - E[Y | do(Diabetes=0), G] for G = focal children aged 6-9 yrs at the sibling's onset

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). Split by the focal child's age at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset; this column keeps focal children aged 6-9 yrs at onset, an age at which Danish children are primary school (grades zero through three).
population.ages: focal child aged 6-9 yrs at the sibling's (pseudo) T1D onset
subgroups_defined: focal child's age at the sibling's onset: 6-9 yrs
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

lhs: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

implies_edges.from: Diabetes (sibling diagnosed with T1D before the focal child turns 16)
implies_edges.to: focal child's outcomes before the sibling's diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)
a socio-economic gradient in T1D onset
pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed
robustness_checks: estimates reported with and without covariate adjustment (Table 3)
balance test of the conditioning set with a joint F-test (Table 2)
falsification test using focal children whose sibling is diagnosed after the 9th grade Exit Exam (Table 4)
inclusion of matched group fixed effects (results not shown; available from the authors upon request)
Oster (2019) omitted-variable-bias methodology (results not shown; available upon request)

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

population.description: Matched sample of focal children: Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling, not themselves diagnosed with T1D, from families with at most one sibling diagnosed with T1D and with sibling spacing of at most five years; 13,752 children, of which 16.67 percent have a sibling diagnosed with T1D (2,292 treated, 11,460 control). population.ages: survey responses in 2015-2017, in grades four through nine
population.selection: Focal children are Danish native singletons born 1988-2002 with at least one sibling; focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed with T1D are dropped (0.61% of the sample), and the sample is restricted to sibling pairs born at most five years apart. Each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size. The sample is not conditioned on having taken the Danish or mathematics exam.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the incidence and timing of type 1 diabetes onset among the siblings of focal children, treated as a quasi-random disability shock; each treated focal child is matched without replacement to five untreated focal children on birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.

key_assumptions.assumption: Quasi-random onset / conditional ignorability: T1D is an unforeseeable disability shock whose unknown origin is unrelated to anything that would independently impact educational outcomes, so that, conditional on the matching variables (birth year, sibling spacing, completed family size) and the included covariates, having a sibling diagnosed with T1D is independent of the focal child's potential educational outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Low inheritability of T1D (2-3% risk for children of mothers with T1D, 5% for fathers); no socio-economic gradient in onset (Praetorius, Urhoj & Andersen, 2022); no pre-onset differences in income, APGAR scores, birthweight or health-care use (Eriksen et al., 2021, 2023); similar school absenteeism 12 to 5 months before diagnosis (Fig. 1); the balance test and joint F-test in Table 2; and the falsification test in Table 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the onset of T1D is sudden, with symptoms severe enough to affect school absenteeism only from about four months before diagnosis, so the sibling's future diagnosis does not affect the focal child's outcomes before onset.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 (reproduced from Thingholm et al., 2020): school absenteeism of the diagnosed child is similar 12 to 5 months prior to clinical diagnosis and rises only from about four months before onset.

key_assumptions.assumption: No undiagnosed treatment in the control group: because it is impossible to survive untreated with T1D, control focal children do not have siblings with undiagnosed T1D.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Clinical argument that T1D cannot go undiagnosed (Hakim et al., 2010), plus complete coverage of the DanDiabKids clinical register.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / exact matching on the matching variables: each treated focal child can be matched without replacement to five untreated focal children with the same birth year, sibling spacing and completed family size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 3,068 of 3,070 children with a sibling with T1D could be matched; Table 1 shows identical means of the three matching variables in the treated and control groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on the focal child's own health and background: focal children diagnosed with T1D themselves are deleted, families where more than one sibling is diagnosed are dropped, non-natives are excluded and sibling spacing is restricted to at most five years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample-construction steps (pp. 4-5); the paper motivates each exclusion (own T1D affects exam performance; immigrant children have different educational progress; widely spaced siblings interact less).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across matched groups: one family's sibling diagnosis does not affect the educational outcomes of focal children in other families.

threats_discussed: the unknown cause of T1D could itself be related to educational outcomes (i.e. these children would perform worse even without the sibling's diagnosis)
inheritability of T1D (parents or the focal child in worse health)

pre-existing differences in the siblings' underlying health that would have required reallocation of parental resources anyway
unobservable differences between families where a child will be diagnosed and families where no child will be diagnosed
